title: Full request path (client to target)
hook: Tracing one HTTPS request from a browser through Domain Name System (DNS), Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, an Application Load Balancer (ALB), security groups, and finally to an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) or Elastic Container Service (ECS) target is the perimeter interview capstone — every hop has rules that can drop traffic.

blocks.text: A typical public web API path: Route53 resolves app.example.com to CloudFront; CloudFront terminates TLS and forwards to an ALB origin (or Lambda@Edge); AWS WAF Web ACL filters at CloudFront or ALB; ALB listener rules route to a target group; security groups on ALB ENI and target ENI must both allow the flow; Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) on subnets optionally filter. Response path reverses with stateful SG return and stateless NACL outbound rules.

blocks.text: 503 errors without logs often mean a hop silently dropped traffic — wrong security group, WAF block, or target failing health checks. Senior interviews ask you to narrate the full path and which diagnostic tool applies per hop: WAF sampled requests, ALB access logs, VPC Flow Logs, target application logs.

blocks.title: Debug order
blocks.body: DNS resolves? CloudFront/WAF block? ALB healthy targets? SG chain ALB→target? App listening on port?

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: DNS
items.body: Client resolves app.example.com → CloudFront edge or Route53 alias to ALB.

items.title: TLS at edge
items.body: CloudFront or ALB terminates HTTPS; certificate from ACM.

items.title: WAF evaluation
items.body: Web ACL rules allow or block before origin fetch.

items.title: ALB routing
items.body: Listener rule forwards to target group; health checks gate targets.

items.title: SG + NACL
items.body: ALB SG allows 443 inbound; target SG allows 8080 from ALB SG; NACL stateless rules if custom.

items.title: Application
items.body: Node/Express or NestJS handles HTTP; response reverses path.

diagram.title: Full request path
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant R as Route53
  participant CF as CloudFront
  participant W as AWS WAF
  participant A as ALB
  participant S as Security groups
  participant T as ECS target
  C->>R: DNS query
  R-->>C: CloudFront IP
  C->>CF: HTTPS GET /api/orders
  CF->>W: Evaluate Web ACL
  W->>A: Forward on allow
  A->>S: Check ALB/target SGs
  S->>T: HTTP to port 8080
  T-->>C: JSON response

snippet.label: CloudFormation — CloudFront to ALB with WAF
snippet.code:
Distribution:
  Type: AWS::CloudFront::Distribution
  Properties:
    DistributionConfig:
      WebACLId: !GetAtt CloudFrontWebAcl.Arn
      Origins:
        - Id: alb-origin
          DomainName: !GetAtt Alb.DNSName
          CustomOriginConfig:
            OriginProtocolPolicy: https-only
      DefaultCacheBehavior:
        TargetOriginId: alb-origin
        ViewerProtocolPolicy: redirect-to-https
        AllowedMethods: [GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE]
        CachePolicyId: 4135ea2d-6df8-44a3-9df3-4b5a84be39ad
snippet.explanation: Managed CachingDisabled policy for dynamic APIs. WAF Web ACL ID on distribution for edge filtering.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: CloudFront origin protocol HTTP to ALB that only listens HTTPS. ALB security group allows 443 but target SG blocks ALB SG on app port. Caching enabled on POST /api/* — stale or broken mutations.

blocks.text: CloudFront origin-facing security group should allow only CloudFront managed prefix list (or use Origin Access Control for S3). ALB preserves X-Forwarded-For; trust proxy settings in Express/NestJS matter for audit logs. How to prove it in production: end-to-end synthetic canary in CloudWatch Synthetics; correlate ALB request count with WAF AllowedRequests; Flow Logs on target subnet during incident.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: No edge cache; origin exposed to global clients
Different path — no ALB target SG chain

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Stopping at 'check security groups' without naming every hop. Strong answer: DNS → CloudFront → WAF → ALB listener → target group health → dual SG chain → NACL if custom → app — with the right diagnostic per layer.

interviewTakeaways: Full path: Route53 → CloudFront → WAF → ALB → security groups → target (ECS/EC2).
WAF can block before origin; unhealthy targets cause ALB 502 without app logs.
Both ALB SG and target SG must allow the flow; NACL outbound ephemeral if custom NACL.
60s: Narrate each hop. DNS first. Edge TLS and WAF. ALB routes to healthy targets. SG chain is top cause of silent drops. Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer prove path.
Follow-up: how does Origin Access Control change the S3 origin path?
commonPitfalls: Debugging only application logs when WAF blocked at edge — gets you rejected; no request reached origin.
Strong answer: check WAF metrics and sampled requests before SSH to EC2.
Target SG allows 0.0.0.0/0 instead of ALB SG reference.
CloudFront caching dynamic API responses — users see stale data after deploy.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express app.set('trust proxy', true) needed behind ALB/CloudFront for accurate client IP in logs — without it, req.ip shows ALB private IP.
NestJS /health should hit dependencies lightly — ALB health check failures drain targets before TypeScript exceptions appear in user-facing 502s.
